lessons.title: Scaling Up: From Maquette to Monument
lessons.body: A maquette is a small model, usually 1:10 or 1:20 scale. To scale up, you need a grid system. Build a wooden frame around your maquette and stretch string across it every 5 cm horizontally and vertically. This creates a coordinate grid. For the full-size sculpture, build a similar frame but with string every 50 cm (if 1:10 scale). Transfer each point where the sculpture touches a grid line. Use a plumb bob to check vertical alignment. For complex curves, take cross-sections: slice the maquette virtually at intervals, measure the profile, and cut cardboard templates. These templates guide bending and welding. In Africa, use locally available materials: mild steel rods (6mm, 8mm, 12mm) from hardware stores in Nairobi or Lagos. A common mistake is to scale only the height; you must scale all three dimensions. If your maquette is 30 cm tall and you want a 3 m sculpture, multiply every measurement by 10. Keep a scaling factor chart. For very large works, use a pantograph or a digital projector to cast the maquette's shadow onto a wall, then trace. But remember, shadows distort; better to use the grid. Start by building a sturdy workbench at least 2 m x 1 m. Clamp your maquette securely. Use calipers to measure small details. For the full-size, you will need a MIG welder (180-250 amps) and an angle grinder. Work in sections: scale up the legs first, then the torso, then the head. Weld temporary braces to keep shapes from warping. Check against the maquette every hour. If you are in a rural area without electricity, use a generator (5-7 kVA) or oxy-acetylene welding. Always wear a welding helmet, gloves, and leather apron. This process takes patience: a 3 m sculpture might take 2-3 weeks of full-time work. But with a good grid, you will achieve accuracy within 1-2 cm.

lessons.title: Armatures and Internal Support Structures
lessons.body: An armature is the skeleton inside a sculpture. For large metal works, it must support the weight of the metal skin, resist wind (in open air), and allow for expansion. Use mild steel for the core: 12mm or 16mm round bars for main supports, 8mm for cross-bracing. For a 4 m tall figure, a central spine of 20mm pipe (schedule 40) works well. Weld a base plate (10mm thick, 300x300mm) to the bottom of the spine. This plate will bolt to a concrete foundation. Add horizontal ribs every 50 cm: these are 8mm bars bent to follow the cross-section shape. Weld them to the spine. Then add diagonal bracing (6mm bars) in a zigzag pattern to prevent twisting. For a human figure, the armature should have separate supports for arms and legs: use 12mm bars that extend from the spine outward. At joints (shoulders, hips), reinforce with gusset plates (5mm thick). If the sculpture will be outdoors, drill 10mm drainage holes at the lowest points of hollow sections to let rainwater out. For coastal areas (like Mombasa or Dakar), use galvanized or stainless steel for critical parts, or coat with zinc-rich primer. A common failure is insufficient anchoring: the armature must be strong enough that a person can hang from any point without bending. Test by applying a 50 kg load at the extremities. For abstract works, use a truss system: two parallel pipes connected by zigzag bars. This is light and strong. Remember, the armature will be hidden, so focus on strength, not beauty. But keep it accessible for future maintenance: leave a small hatch or removable panel. In Africa, recycled materials work: old bed frames, car axles, and scaffolding pipes are excellent. Clean them with a wire brush and grinder before welding. Always weld in a well-ventilated area; galvanized steel produces toxic fumes. If using recycled steel, test for weldability with a small bead first.

lessons.title: Transportation and Installation Logistics
lessons.body: Moving a large sculpture requires planning. First, calculate weight: steel weighs 7.85 kg per meter for 1 cmÂ² cross-section. A 4 m sculpture with 12mm bars and 3mm sheet might weigh 300-500 kg. For transport, you need a truck with a flatbed or a low-bed trailer. In many African cities, hire a 7-ton truck (e.g., Isuzu FRR) for local moves. For inter-city, use a 10-ton truck. Secure the sculpture with ratchet straps (5-ton capacity) at four points. Protect delicate parts with blankets or cardboard. If the sculpture is taller than 4 m, you may need a police escort and a route survey to avoid low bridges and power lines. For installation, you need a mobile crane or a truck-mounted crane. A 5-ton crane can lift 500 kg at 3 m radius. Book the crane for at least 4 hours. Prepare the foundation in advance: a concrete pad (minimum 1 m x 1 m x 1 m for a 500 kg sculpture) with anchor bolts (M20) set in place. Use a template to ensure bolts match the base plate. On installation day, lift the sculpture slowly. Use tag lines (ropes) to control rotation. Lower onto the bolts, then secure with nuts and washers. Check verticality with a spirit level. If the sculpture is in a public space, you may need permits from the city council (e.g., Nairobi City County) and possibly the roads authority. Allow 2-4 weeks for permits. For remote sites, consider assembling on-site: weld sections together after transport. This reduces transport size. Always have a backup plan: if the crane fails, can you use a forklift or a block and tackle? For very heavy works, hire a rigging company. Document everything with photos and videos for your portfolio. Insurance is wise: transit insurance and public liability. Typical costs: truck hire $200-$500, crane $300-$800 per day, permits $50-$200. Budget 10% extra for contingencies.

lessons.title: Public Art: Proposal Writing and Permitting
lessons.body: A public art proposal must convince a committee. Start with a one-page summary: title, concept, dimensions, materials, budget, timeline. Then a detailed section: concept statement (why this sculpture for this site), design sketches (3-5 views), maquette photos, and a site plan showing placement. Include a budget breakdown: materials (steel, paint, concrete), labour (your time and assistants), equipment (crane, welder), transport, permits, insurance, and a 15% contingency. For a 3 m sculpture, typical budget in Africa: materials $800-$1500, labour $1000-$2000, equipment $500-$1000, permits $100-$300, total $2400-$4800. Add your artist fee (20-30% of costs). Write a maintenance plan: how to clean, repaint, and inspect. Include a timeline: design (2 weeks), fabrication (4-6 weeks), installation (1 week). For permits, contact the local council's arts and culture department. In Kenya, you need a permit from the county government and possibly the National Museums of Kenya if the site is heritage. In Nigeria, state arts councils. In South Africa, local municipalities. Provide a site map, proof of landowner permission (e.g., letter from the mall or park), and your ID. Fees vary: $50-$200. For private commissions (hotels, malls), the process is simpler: just a contract. Always get a written agreement specifying payment schedule (e.g., 30% deposit, 40% on approval of maquette, 30% on installation). Include a clause for changes: extra work billed at hourly rate. For public art, you may need to present to a community board. Prepare a 5-minute pitch and answer questions. Show you understand the site: sun direction, wind, pedestrian flow. Propose a sculpture that is safe: no sharp edges, stable, and resistant to climbing. If children can reach it, ensure no gaps that trap heads. Finally, submit a digital portfolio with previous work. Even if you have none, show your maquette and drawings. Persistence pays: it may take 3-5 proposals before you win a commission.

lessons.title: Collaboration with Engineers and Fabricators
lessons.body: You are the artist, but for large-scale work you need engineers and specialist fabricators. A structural engineer can calculate wind loads and foundation sizes. For a 5 m sculpture in a windy area, wind load can be 1.5 kN/mÂ². The engineer will tell you the required base plate thickness and anchor bolt size. In Africa, find engineers through local universities (e.g., Makerere, University of Nairobi) or professional bodies (IEK, ECSA). Expect to pay $200-$500 for a stamped drawing. For fabrication, you may need a workshop with a 5-ton overhead crane, a plasma cutter, and a large MIG welder. In cities like Johannesburg, Lagos, or Nairobi, there are metal fabrication shops that can cut, bend, and weld to your specifications. Provide them with detailed shop drawings: every part dimensioned, with weld symbols. Use a CAD program like AutoCAD or free alternatives like LibreCAD. If you can't draw, make a full-size cardboard template and trace onto steel. When working with a fabricator, agree on tolerances: Â±2 mm for critical joints. Visit the shop daily to check progress. For specialised tasks like casting bronze, find a foundry. In West Africa, the Igun Street foundries in Benin City, Nigeria, are famous for lost-wax casting. For stainless steel, look for workshops that do kitchen equipment. Always get a written quote and timeline. Pay 50% deposit, 50% on delivery. Keep a communication log: emails, WhatsApp messages. If the fabricator makes a mistake, be calm but firm: show the drawing and ask for correction. For complex curves, consider using a CNC plasma table; many shops have them. If not, use a template and hand-cut with a plasma torch. Remember, engineers and fabricators are partners, not servants. Respect their expertise. They may suggest cheaper or stronger methods. For example, they might recommend using a truss instead of a solid plate. Listen, but ensure the artistic vision is preserved. Build a team you can rely on for future projects.

lessons.title: Project: Proposal for a Public Sculpture
lessons.body: For this project, you will create a complete proposal for a public sculpture of your design. Choose a real site in your community: a roundabout, park, school, or market square. The sculpture must be at least 2 m tall and made of metal. Follow these steps: 1) Site analysis: visit the site, take photos, note sun direction, wind, pedestrian traffic, and existing structures. Measure available space. 2) Concept: write a 200-word statement explaining what the sculpture represents and why it suits the site. 3) Maquette: build a 1:10 scale model using wire, cardboard, or clay. Photograph it from multiple angles. 4) Drawings: produce a dimensioned sketch of the front, side, and top views. Include a site plan showing placement. 5) Budget: list materials (steel bars, sheet, paint, concrete), labour (your hours at a fair rate, e.g., $10/hour), equipment (welder, grinder, crane), transport, permits, and a 15% contingency. For a 2 m sculpture, aim for a total of $1500-$3000. 6) Timeline: a Gantt chart showing weeks for design, fabrication, and installation. 7) Permitting: identify the office you need to contact (e.g., county arts department) and draft a cover letter. 8) Maintenance: describe how to clean and inspect annually. 9) Presentation: compile everything into a PDF (max 10 pages). If you don't have a computer, make a physical folder with printed pages and drawings. 10) Submit to your instructor for feedback. This project simulates a real commission. You can also present it to your local council for actual consideration. Many public sculptures in Africa started as student projects. Be bold: your proposal could become a landmark. Remember, the best proposals are clear, visual, and realistic. Avoid overpromising. Show you can deliver. Include a photo of yourself with your maquette to personalise it. This project is your portfolio piece. It proves you can think like a professional artist.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a grid system when scaling up a maquette?
options: A) To make the maquette look bigger
B) To transfer measurements accurately from small to large
C) To hold the maquette together
quiz.explanation: A grid allows you to map points from the small model to the full-size sculpture proportionally.

quiz.q: If your maquette is 20 cm tall and you want a 4 m sculpture, what is the scaling factor?
quiz.explanation: 4 m = 400 cm; 400 cm / 20 cm = 20, so the factor is 20.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for checking vertical alignment when scaling up?
quiz.explanation: A plumb bob uses gravity to indicate a true vertical line.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when scaling up?
quiz.explanation: All three dimensions must be scaled proportionally, not just height.

quiz.q: Which material is commonly used for armatures in Africa due to availability?
quiz.explanation: Recycled steel like bed frames is cheap and weldable, ideal for armatures.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of diagonal bracing in an armature?
quiz.explanation: Diagonal bracing resists torsional forces and keeps the structure rigid.

quiz.q: Why should you drill drainage holes in hollow sections?
options: A) To let water out and prevent rust
quiz.explanation: Trapped water causes internal corrosion; drainage holes let it escape.

quiz.q: For a coastal area, what material is best for critical armature parts?
quiz.explanation: Galvanized or stainless steel resists saltwater corrosion better than mild steel.

quiz.q: How can you test the strength of an armature?
options: A) Hit it with a hammer
B) Hang a 50 kg load from extremities
quiz.explanation: Applying a load simulates stress and reveals weak points.

quiz.q: What is a truss system in armature construction?
options: B) Two parallel pipes with zigzag bracing
quiz.explanation: A truss is a lightweight, strong structure made of parallel members and diagonal braces.

quiz.q: What is the weight of steel per meter for a 1 cmÂ² cross-section?
quiz.explanation: Steel density is 7.85 g/cmÂ³, so a 1 cmÂ² bar one meter long weighs 7.85 kg.

quiz.q: Which truck size is typically used for local transport of a 500 kg sculpture?
quiz.explanation: A 7-ton truck provides ample capacity and is commonly available.

quiz.q: What is the minimum concrete foundation size for a 500 kg sculpture?
options: B) 1 m x 1 m x 1 m
C) 2 m x 2 m x 2 m
D) 3 m x 3 m x 3 m
quiz.explanation: A 1 mÂ³ concrete pad provides sufficient weight and stability for a 500 kg sculpture.

quiz.q: What should you use to control rotation during crane lifting?
options: D) Ropes tied to the crane
quiz.explanation: Tag lines are ropes held by workers to guide the load without touching it.

quiz.q: How long should you allow for permits for a public sculpture in a city?
quiz.explanation: Bureaucratic processes typically take 2-4 weeks for approval.

quiz.q: What is a typical cost for crane hire per day in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Crane rental ranges from $300 to $800 per day depending on size and location.

quiz.q: What should a public art proposal include first?
quiz.explanation: A concise summary grabs attention and outlines the key points.

quiz.q: What percentage contingency is recommended in a budget?
quiz.explanation: A 15% contingency covers unexpected costs without overpricing.

quiz.q: In Kenya, which office issues permits for public art?
quiz.explanation: County governments handle local arts and culture permits.

quiz.q: What is a typical artist fee as a percentage of costs?
quiz.explanation: Artist fees usually range from 20% to 30% of the total project cost.

quiz.q: What is a key safety consideration for public art accessible to children?
options: B) No gaps that trap heads
quiz.explanation: Design must prevent entrapment hazards, especially for children.

quiz.q: What is the role of a structural engineer in large-scale sculpture?
options: B) To calculate wind loads and foundation sizes
quiz.explanation: Engineers ensure the sculpture can withstand environmental forces.

quiz.q: What is a typical wind load for a 5 m sculpture in a windy area?
quiz.explanation: Wind loads around 1.5 kN/mÂ² are common for exposed sites.

quiz.q: Where can you find lost-wax casting foundries in West Africa?
quiz.explanation: Igun Street in Benin City, Nigeria, is famous for traditional lost-wax casting.

quiz.q: What should you provide to a fabricator for complex parts?
quiz.explanation: Shop drawings with dimensions and weld symbols ensure accurate fabrication.

quiz.q: What is a common tolerance for critical joints in metal fabrication?
quiz.explanation: Â±2 mm is a reasonable tolerance for structural joints.

quiz.q: What is the recommended deposit for a fabrication job?
quiz.explanation: A 50% deposit covers material costs and secures the job.

quiz.q: What is the minimum height for the project sculpture?
quiz.explanation: The project requires a sculpture at least 2 m tall.

quiz.q: What should be included in the site analysis?
quiz.explanation: Site analysis covers environmental factors affecting the sculpture.

quiz.q: What is the final deliverable for the project?
options: A) A PDF or physical folder with proposal
quiz.explanation: The project is a proposal, not the actual sculpture.
